# Model card: Reference summary

| | |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Summarise submitted references: themes, strengths, development areas and contradictions between referees. |
| Workflow | hire |
| Code | `pairly_hire.references.summary` |
| Prompt | `hire_reference_summary` version `v1`, file SHA-256 `561fb5c36b6a53f9...` |
| Output schema | `ReferenceDraft` |
| Model tiers, cheapest first | `small` (anthropic `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, openai `gpt-6-luna`) then `large` (anthropic `claude-sonnet-5-5`, openai `gpt-6.1-sol`) |
| Temperature | 0.0 |
| Output token limit | 1200 |
| Confidence threshold to accept | none |

## Inputs

The job title, the language and, per reference, a label and the answers. Never the referee's name or address, never the CV. Redacted first while the candidate is blind.

## Outputs

A `ReferenceDraft`. Consistency with the CV is checked in code, not by the model.

## Human oversight

The hiring team reads the summary next to the answers and decides.

## Limits

* Summaries can flatten nuance in a referee's wording.
* A refused or failed draft falls back to a deterministic template.
* Every call is logged in `model_calls` (prompt version and hash, model, inputs, output, tokens, cost) and fails closed: no model means a person does the step.

Structural checks only (`python -m evals.structural`), on the committed recordings: scripted answers, not model output. They say whether every recorded output fits the schema, holds no banned content or em dash, passes the component's own deterministic check and points only at its input. They are not quality judgments: how good a draft is needs a live model and people.
